sections.html: The golden dwarf cichlid, Nannacara anomala, ranges from the Rio Aruka in Guyana to the lower Rio Marowijne in Suriname. It is often found in flooded grassland in low-lying coastal areas, but most fish in the trade are mass-produced on farms in the Far East or Eastern Europe. Hardy and easy to breed, it is regarded as an excellent beginner's cichlid, though a female guarding fry can be very aggressive.

The natural range of this species extends from the Rio Aruka in Guyana to the lower Rio Marowijne in Suriname. Most of the ones in the trade are mass-produced on commercial farms in the Far East or Eastern Europe.
Often found inhabiting areas of flooded grassland in low-lying coastal areas.

Standard length: 7.6 cm SL.

Aquarium base: 46 × 38 cm. Volume: approximately 52 litres (46 × 38 × 30 cm).
Provide a well planted setup with bits of bogwood, driftwood or mopani wood to provide cover and spawning sites for these fish.

• Temperature: 22–27°C
  • pH: Acidic, but can tolerate moderately alkaline: 6 to 7.5
  • Hardness: Prefer soft, but can tolerate moderately hard: 3 to 8 dGH

It's naturally a micropredator, foraging for worms, insects and other invertebrates in the wild. Anomala should take dry foods, in which case a meaty cichlid pellet should be fed as staple food. Make sure the diet is supplemented with both vegetative matter (vegetable/spirulina flakes or small pieces of cucumber) and frozen/live foods (of which the Anomala will prefer bloodworm and brine shrimp).

Very peaceful dwarf cichlid. Can be kept in a community with most other peaceful fish. The female can be very aggressive indeed when protecting her fry, so if the Nannacara anomala start breeding in a community tank you may have problems.

The male is much bigger, generally exhibiting pale blues and reds, whilst the smaller female tends to be yellow with a black lateral line on her flank. The female will present a checkerboard-like pattern when in breeding mood.

Very simple. In merely adequate water conditions, a single male and female will very likely breed. Breeding is even easier in a larger tank with a number of females providing companionship to a single male. Females require "sub-territories" of at least 40 × 40 cm on the bottom of a tank, so a 76 cm tank would be required to house two females with a male.

Nannacara anomala are widely available in the trade, and are generally regarded as an excellent beginner's fish. If a beginner is interested in keeping cichlids and learning about breeding, then these fish are absolutely ideal. Anomala are attractive, hardy and usually quite cheap to purchase. Like some species of the Apistogramma genus, the mother may use fascinating body language to communicate with her fry when she is caring for them. If there is more than one male in a tank smaller than 120 cm, the subdominant male may take on the guise of a female (colouration and size) to avoid the aggression of the dominant male. If the dominant male was taken away, the subdominant male would quickly (a matter of weeks) grow into a fully functioning male and become the dominant male in the tank. "Nannacara" simply means "Small Acara".
